title: God and Philosophy
author: Van Bryan
summary: Prompted by John Burnet's Early Greek Philosophy, Van Bryan surveys how spirituality shaped early Greek thought and what relationship religion had with the study of philosophy. He moves through the Milesians' search for an arche that they sometimes called divine, Pythagoras's religious sect and wheel of rebirth, Xenophanes's critique of anthropomorphic gods, and Plato's eternal soul and world of the forms. The recurring move is to show that ideas central to later religions were first argued for as metaphysical or epistemological conclusions rather than religious ones. Bryan concludes that ancient philosophy and spirituality were good-natured rivals that sometimes reached the same conclusions by very different routes. The piece is an accessible introduction to the Presocratics and Plato for general readers of the classics.
points: The Milesians used the word God in a largely secular way while seeking the single primordial substance beneath reality.
Pythagoras not only embraced spirituality but required his followers to keep strict religious practices.
Xenophanes argued that if horses could draw, they would draw gods like horses, and he is often called the first Western monotheist intellectual.
Plato's arguments for an immortal soul and the world of the forms later appealed to Christian theologians, though Plato framed them philosophically.
quotes: This article is not so much an examination of theology nor the philosophy of religion...instead, I hope we can take a look back through the centuries of ancient philosophy and see what impact spirituality has had on the development of ancient thought and what type of relationship religion had with the study of philosophy.
Now what is interesting about all of this is that while attempting to uncover this first substance, the philosophers would often attribute divine importance to the arche

Unlike the Milesians, Pythagoras not only embraced spirituality, he actually demanded it. His followers were required to adhere to a strict set of religious traditions if they wished to remain within the sect.

The conclusion that Xenophanes draws is that God, if indeed there is a God, would be wholly unlike the humans of this world. God would not be fallible, corporeal, or even intelligible. In short, God would be beyond our comprehension.

It is important to keep in mind that Plato’s idea of the transmigration of the soul and the world of the forms was not a religious one. To Plato, it was the basis of his metaphysical and epistemological philosophy.

While science and religion appear to be very much at odds today, there once was a time when they were considered to overlap. The ancient philosophers went in pursuit of answers and often came up with answers that are strikingly similar to modern-day religious beliefs.

So I suppose we could consider ancient philosophy and spirituality to be good-natured rivals. They get along in some respects; they disagree at other times. Occasionally, they will come to the same conclusion. The manner in which they reach these conclusions, however, is vastly different.
